finding.claim: Unauthenticated cross-tenant user enumeration: GET /users returns id and name for any org chosen by the caller via req.query.org, with no auth, tenant binding, or pagination.
finding.sink: SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE org = $1 (db.js:9), rows returned as JSON (db.js:10)

trace.note: app.listen(3002) serves all routes with no auth middleware
GET /users registered with no auth or session check
all matching rows returned as JSON

finding.guards_checked: Query is parameterized (no SQLi). No auth, session, or tenant-membership check in file. No pagination or row cap. Org not bound to caller identity.

verdict.guard_found: none. db.js:8 registers GET /users with no auth, session, or tenant check; db.js:9 binds req.query.org directly as $1; db.js:10 returns all rows as JSON; db.js:23 listens on 3002 with no auth middleware. No other code files exist in the directory (the .claude/skills/*.md files are docs, not middleware). The parameterized query prevents SQL injection but does not stop cross-tenant enumeration.
verdict.reason: An anonymous HTTP caller can choose any org via req.query.org at db.js:9 and receive every matching id and name at db.js:10, with no control between them at db.js:8 or db.js:23. Caveat: req.pg is never set in this codebase, so as written the handler throws at db.js:9 and returns nothing; the leak becomes real once a pg-providing middleware is added, which the finding does not mention.

finding.claim: Unhandled async rejection in /users handler can crash the process (availability). Conditional on Express 4 and on req.pg being absent or the DB erroring.
finding.source: Any unauthenticated request to /users; req.pg is never attached in this file, and DB errors propagate
finding.sink: await req.pg.query(...) (db.js:9) rejects inside async handler (db.js:8) with no try/catch or next(err)

trace.note: async handler with no error handling
req.pg.query throws TypeError if req.pg is undefined, or rejects on DB error
Express 4 does not catch async rejections, so Node raises unhandledRejection, which terminates the process on Node 15+

finding.guards_checked: No try/catch, no .catch(), no error middleware in file, no process.on('unhandledRejection') handler. Express version unknown (no package.json).

verdict.guard_found: none. db.js has no try/catch, no .catch(), no error middleware, and no process.on('unhandledRejection') handler. Nothing in the directory attaches req.pg, so `req.pg.query` at db.js:9 throws a TypeError inside the async handler at db.js:8. The only other guards, the path check at db.js:15 and the 403 at db.js:15, belong to /file and do not apply to /users.
verdict.reason: The async handler at db.js:8 awaits `req.pg.query` at db.js:9 with no error handling, and nothing in the directory sets `req.pg`, so any anonymous GET /users throws, and under Express 4 (which does not forward async rejections to next) the rejection becomes an unhandled rejection that crashes Node 15+ (db.js:8-9). The verdict assumes Express 4, which the candidate itself names as the condition; under Express 5 the rejection would be forwarded to the error handler and the crash would not occur. The Express version is not in the repo, so this is the one residual uncertainty.

finding.claim: GET /count spawns a child process per unauthenticated request with no rate limit, and swallows wc errors by returning HTTP 200 with an empty body.
finding.sink: execFile("wc", ["-l","data.csv"]) (db.js:20) and res.send(out) ignoring error e (db.js:20)

trace.note: execFile spawns wc per request; callback ignores e and sends out

finding.guards_checked: No shell used (execFile with fixed argv, no injection). File name is constant. No auth, rate limit, or concurrency cap. Error not checked.

verdict.guard_found: none. db.js:19 registers GET /count with no auth middleware, and no app.use or rate-limit is registered anywhere in db.js. db.js:20 calls execFile with a fixed argv array (no shell), so there is no injection, but the callback ignores the error argument e and sends out unconditionally, so a failed wc returns 200 with an empty body.
verdict.reason: Anonymous clients can reach the unauthenticated GET /count route at db.js:19, which spawns a wc process on every request (db.js:20) with no rate limit or concurrency cap, and the callback at db.js:20 discards e and calls res.send(out), so failures return HTTP 200 with an empty body. The trace is accurate; the impact is low (resource exhaustion and silent error handling, not a data-exposure or injection issue).

finding.claim: Server binds on all interfaces with no auth, exposing all routes (including /users and /file) to any host that can reach port 3002.
finding.sink: app.listen(3002) (db.js:23) with no host argument, so bind is 0.0.0.0 or ::

trace.note: listen(port) with no host binds all interfaces

finding.guards_checked: No bind address configured in code. No proxy, firewall, or auth visible in the repo.

verdict.guard_found: none. No host argument or bind-address config exists in db.js:23 or elsewhere in the repo (the grep for listen/host/bind only matched db.js:23). The /file path check at db.js:15 and the parameterized query at db.js:9 limit other attacks but do not restrict which interfaces accept connections, and no auth exists on /users, /file, or /count.
verdict.reason: db.js:23 calls app.listen(3002) with no host, so Node binds to all interfaces (:: or 0.0.0.0), and nothing in the repo restricts that; whether an external host can actually reach the port depends on deployment (firewall, container, or proxy config), which is not in the repo.

finding.claim: Unauthenticated GET /file with ?name= pointing at a directory inside public/ hits sendFile's error path; the default Express error handler can return a stack trace outside production.
finding.source: Unauthenticated ?name= value naming a directory under public/
finding.sink: res.sendFile(p) with no callback (db.js:16), error forwarded to default error handler

trace.note: prefix check passes because the directory is inside ROOT
sendFile fails on a directory, calls next(err), default handler prints stack

finding.guards_checked: Prefix check at db.js:15 correctly blocks traversal. No error handling for the sendFile failure path.

verdict.guard_found: Prefix check at db.js:15 (p.startsWith(ROOT + path.sep)) blocks traversal outside public/ but allows directories inside it, so it does not stop this path. No callback or error handler on res.sendFile at db.js:16, so failures reach Express's default handler. No auth middleware on /file (db.js:13-17).
verdict.reason: Anonymous requests reach db.js:16 with a directory name under public/ that passes the check at db.js:15, and nothing at db.js:16 handles the error, so the default handler can print a stack trace when NODE_ENV is not "production"; this is information disclosure only, and any nonexistent name triggers the same leak, so the directory case is not special. Express is not installed in this directory, so the EISDIR-to-next(err) behavior is assumed from Express's source rather than verified here.

finding.claim: ROOT (db.js:6) and data.csv (db.js:20) are resolved relative to process.cwd(), not the script location, so the served tree and the counted file change with the launch directory.
finding.source: Process working directory at startup (deployment configuration, not attacker input)
finding.sink: path.resolve("public") (db.js:6) used as the /file root; relative "data.csv" (db.js:20) used by wc

trace.note: wc reads data.csv relative to cwd

finding.guards_checked: None. Deployment-dependent logic issue, not attacker-controlled.

verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: db.js:6 uses path.resolve("public") and db.js:20 runs execFile("wc", ["-l", "data.csv"]) with no cwd option, so both depend on process.cwd(). But the attacker cannot influence the launch directory, so nothing attacker-reachable is affected; this is a deployment-configuration robustness issue, not a vulnerability.
